newsitem.title: USA: NYC needs to pay debt with recurring revs - official.
newsitem.headline: NYC needs to pay debt with recurring revs - official.

text.p: New York City needs to develop a plan that relies on recurring revenues to pay for its debt, rather than one shot revenues and other non-recurring resources, State Deputy Comptroller for New York City Rosemary Scanlon said Tuesday.

Scanlon, testifying at the city's Office of Management and Budget on the city's debt affordability, said, "The city has yet to demonstrate that its forecasted debt burden is ultimately affordable along with other expense budget needs over an extended period, since in past years the city has relied extensively on non-recurring resources which have only temporarily reduced debt service costs."

"Such resources have included the proceeds from the sale of assets, and savings from refunding bonds," said Scanlon, who is a member of the city's Financial Control Board and represents one of the official fiscal monitors of the city's finances. "In my opinion, the city needs to be able to fund debt service with recurring revenues."
Scanlon noted the city shows a high and rising debt burden over the fiscal year 1996 through fiscal year 2001 period.

"For example, debt service as a percent of total taxes, a commonly cited benchmark, grows from 14.6 percent in fiscal year 1996, on a gross basis, to 20 percent in fiscal year 1999, a level that it essentially holds though 2000 and 2001," Scanlon said.

Even after adjusting for the use of non-recurring revenues to pay debt service, debt service grows by 7.1 percent annualy from fiscal year 1996 to fiscal year 2001, she said. This compares to the projected growth in tax revenues over this period of 2.1 percent annually.

"The level of outstanding debt is forecast to grow from $30 billion at the end of fiscal year 1996, to nearly $37 billion by the end of fiscal year 2001," Scanlon said. "Should the city's population remain largely unchanged as the city forecasts, the debt load for each city resident would grow to more than $5,000 in 2001."
Scanlon also noted that over the fiscal year 1986-fiscal year 1997 period, "questionable debt practices have added approximatley $2.9 billion in oustanding city debt."
For example, most GO bond refunding during this period were carried out primarily to produce short-term budgetary gains.
And analysis by the comptroller's office shows that hese refundings added on average some $200 million per year to debt service costs over the FY 1996 through 2007 period.
The sale of most assets was not used to retire debt, even though the asset was financed with debt, Scanlon said.

And the city had planned to pay from some capital expenses on a pay-as-you-go basis, using surpluses from the sale of WNYC-TV and refundings by the Municipal Assistance Corporation for the City of New York. However, the city has since decided to use bonding for these projects and the surpluses for operating expenses, Scanlon said. It provided short-term budget relief, but added costs over the long-term.

"In my opinion, a preferable course for the city would have been to use all or a portion of these resources to either retire or defease outstanding debt or to fund a portion of the capital budget on a pay-as-you-go basis," Scanlon said. "This would have reduced both the level of outstanding debt and the debt service burden." --U.S. Municipal Desk, 212-859-1650
